title: The unwholesome four
hook: delusion, shamelessness, recklessness, restlessness: present in every unwholesome moment

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven in every moment: contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life and attention. Your line: seven always. Which tones did you catch? Day one thousand seventy-four.

"As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind." That's a verse from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation. A roof with gaps doesn't look like trouble on a dry afternoon. It shows itself when the weather turns, one drip at a time, right over the bed. Today the Abhidhamma points at the gaps. It names four factors it finds in every unwholesome moment of mind, whatever else is going on in it.
screen: `AN ILL-THATCHED HOUSE.` → `THE GAPS SHOW IN THE RAIN.` → `FOUR GAPS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Unwholesome translates akusala, the opposite of kusala, skillful or healthy. It is not a verdict on a person. In the suttas, the Buddha tells his son Rahula to look at an action before, during and after it, and to ask one thing: does this lead to harm, for me, for others, or for both? A state that leads to harm is unskillful. That's the test, not a label. Now the four. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha says that whenever a moment is unwholesome, these are present. Delusion, moha: the mind can't see clearly what it's doing, like walking in fog. Shamelessness, ahirika: no inner pull of, this isn't who I want to be. Recklessness, anottappa: no care for what the act will do, to others or to oneself. And restlessness, uddhacca: the mind can't settle, like water stirred by wind. Here is something easy to miss. Greed and anger are not on this list. They come and go, and the manual gives each its own family, which we meet over the next two days. These four sit underneath every unwholesome moment, whether it's a sharp word or a quiet bit of cruelty. And restlessness may be the easiest of the four to feel. On this account, an unwholesome moment is never fully at rest. There is a jitter in it. That makes the teaching practical. Nobody has to diagnose their own heart from the inside. It's enough to feel for agitation, in the jaw, the hands, the speed of the next thought. Where the roof jitters, rain is getting in. Later this week, the manual shows the other side: two factors that are exact opposites of shamelessness and recklessness.
screen: `UNSKILLFUL, NOT A VERDICT.` · `FOG, NO SHAME, NO CARE, NO REST.` · `GREED AND ANGER: THEIR OWN FAMILIES.` · then, large: `FEEL FOR THE JITTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: notice restlessness. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Then feel for any restlessness at all: a foot that wants to jiggle, a mind skipping to the next thing, a pull toward the phone. Don't call it bad. Just find where it lives: the hands, the chest, behind the eyes. Then let one long breath out and see whether it settles a little, or not. Either way, it has been seen, and that is the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
The unwholesome four. Delusion, shamelessness, recklessness and restlessness: the four the manual finds in every unwholesome moment. Today's word.
Your line: the troubled four. Today, let restlessness be a signal. When you feel the jitter, take one breath before the next word, the next text, the next click. Day one thousand seventy-four.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the four unwholesome universals by their Pali names, and some meditation teachers in Theravada communities encourage students to notice restlessness as a sign that an unskillful state is present.

fork.setup: you're building a house in rain country, with a thatched roof, and you're short on time. what do you do?
options: thatch it fast and patch the gaps later.
thatch it well, gap by gap.
skip the roof; it isn't raining yet.
fork.reveal: the Dhammapada's verse: rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, and passion through an unreflecting mind. the gaps only show when the weather turns.

what it means: unskillful, a state that leads to harm; four factors are in every one.

sources.ref: Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ch. 2 (the four unwholesome universals)

notes: The four unwholesome universals (moha, ahirika, anottappa, uddhacca) are from Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 2. 'Recklessness' for anottappa follows the outline; it is often rendered 'fearlessness of wrongdoing' or 'moral recklessness'. Confirm.
'akusala, the opposite of kusala, skillful or healthy' is a translation gloss, not an etymology. Confirm the wording.
MN 61 paraphrased: Rahula reflects on bodily, verbal and mental actions before, during and after, asking whether they lead to affliction of self, others or both.
'like walking in fog' and 'like water stirred by wind' are the writer's images, not presented as commentary similes.
'restlessness is the one that can be felt' and 'an unwholesome moment is never fully at rest' are interpretive, built on uddhacca being present in every unwholesome citta. Confirm the framing.
Editor: fixed the garbled screen line ('have own families'); 'restlessness is the one that can be felt' softened to 'may be the easiest of the four to feel'.
